account: Jessica Cicchino of the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) in Arlington, Virginia, studied police-reported pedestrian crashes in the United States. She compared vehicles with and without automatic emergency braking (AEB) that detects pedestrians, and she used only models on which the system was an optional feature. She estimated crash rates per insured vehicle year and checked them with a second method that compares pedestrian crashes with a crash type that the system cannot affect. Vehicles with the system had a 25% to 27% lower pedestrian crash risk and a 29% to 30% lower pedestrian injury crash risk. Accident Analysis & Prevention published the study online on 14 May 2022. The study found no evidence of a benefit at night on roads without street lighting or at speed limits of 50 mph or more. It also found no evidence of a benefit when the equipped vehicle was turning. The design is observational, and the abstract does not name the makers or describe the detection software.
